name: Timor-Leste
summary: The eastern half of Timor, a Portuguese colony for centuries; invaded by Indonesia in 1975, with a brutal occupation that killed a large share of the population; voted for independence in 1999 and became independent in 2002.

location.value: Eastern half of Timor island, with Dili as capital; the page gives 15,007 km² in one place and 14,874 km² in another, so the figures conflict.

terrain.value: A rugged mountain spine runs along the island, rising to Mount Ramelau (about 2,960 m), with narrow coastal plains around Dili and the south coast.

climate.value: Tropical and monsoonal: a wet season from about December to April and a long dry season, cooler and wetter in the mountains.

resources.value: Offshore oil and gas in the Timor Sea (Bayu-Undan and the undeveloped Greater Sunrise fields), plus coffee grown in the highlands around Ermera.

disasters.value: Floods and landslides in the wet season, such as the floods of Cyclone Seroja in Dili in April 2021; droughts also hit food crops.

population.value: 1,341,737 at the 2022 census; 1,434,991 in the 2026 estimate (infobox).

urbanisation.value: Most people live in rural villages; Dili, the capital on the north coast, is by far the largest town, followed by Baucau.

disease.value: Malaria, dengue and tuberculosis remain problems, and high rates of child malnutrition and stunting are a major health concern.

migration.value: After the 1999 independence vote, militia violence drove about 250,000 people into Indonesian West Timor, and many more fled into the hills.

economicBase.value: The economy relies on oil and foreign aid. The Petroleum Fund (set up in 2005) took in $23 billion from 2005 to 2021, held $19 billion in 2021 and supplies 80% of government spending; coffee was 90% of non-fuel exports in 2013–2019.

tradeRoutes.value: Imports come through Dili and the new Tibar Bay port (opened 2022); gas from Bayu-Undan was piped to Darwin in Australia for export.

moneyAndTax.value: Uses the US dollar as its currency, with locally minted centavo coins; most public spending comes from the Petroleum Fund rather than taxes.

inequality.value: Large gaps between Dili and poorer rural districts, where most people depend on small farms with little cash income.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential republic with a one-chamber National Parliament.

keyRulers.value: Timor-Leste’s leaders since independence in 2002 are not named here.

succession.value: Presidents are elected by popular vote for five-year terms; the prime minister comes from the party or coalition holding a majority in parliament.

institutions.value: The single-chamber National Parliament, the presidency, the courts and the Petroleum Fund, built with heavy UN help until the last mission left in 2012.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between parties led by former resistance leaders, especially FRETILIN and the CNRT, shaped the 2006 crisis and later coalitions.

armyAndTech.value: A small defence force, F-FDTL, grew out of the Falintil guerrilla army; it is lightly armed and supported by a national police force.

majorWars.value: Indonesia invaded on 7 December 1975. The page gives a minimum of 102,800 conflict-related deaths in 1974–1999 (about 18,600 killings and 84,200 excess deaths from hunger and illness); other estimates reach 200,000.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: East Timor (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: East Timor (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Fretilin declared independence in November 1975 and Indonesia invaded in early December (no exact day given); annexation in 1976; deaths 'as high as 200,000' by some estimates; referendum 30 August 1999 with almost four-fifths for independence)

territoryChange.value: A 2018 treaty with Australia fixed the sea border in the Timor Sea; the land territory includes the Oecusse exclave inside West Timor.

alliancesRivals.value: Joined ASEAN as its 11th member in 2025; a member of the Portuguese-speaking CPLP, with close ties to Australia and Indonesia.

inventions.value: No major inventions; the country is better known for keeping alive crafts such as tais weaving.

scienceEducation.value: The National University of Timor-Lorosa’e opened in 2000; schools teach in Tetum and Portuguese, and literacy has risen since independence.

openness.value: Open to trade, aid and foreign investment; it joined the World Trade Organization in 2024.

communicationTransport.value: Narrow mountain roads often blocked by landslides, ferries to Oecusse and Atauro, and an international airport at Dili.

languageWriting.value: Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, Indonesian and English are working languages, and over 15 local languages are spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Sacred houses (uma lulik) with tall thatched roofs, handwoven tais cloth, and Portuguese-era churches and buildings in Dili.

socialStructure.value: A young, mostly rural society organised around clans and sacred houses, with many language groups such as Mambai, Makasae and Fataluku.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity built on the long resistance to occupation, the Catholic Church and the Tetum language.

dailyLife.value: Most families farm maize, rice and cassava in small plots, and coffee picking brings cash in the highlands.

neighbours.value: Indonesia, which shares the land border on Timor island, and Australia across the Timor Sea to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Catholicism became a symbol of resistance.

riseSignals.value: Came under Portuguese influence in the 16th century and stayed a Portuguese colony until 1975.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; independence in 2002 and ASEAN membership in 2025 are its main milestones so far.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: A UN-supervised referendum in August 1999; independence restored on 20 May 2002 (infobox).

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
